definition: Dominance or leadership by one group, nation, or idea over others.
example: For decades the town's only newspaper held a hegemony over local opinion that no newcomer could break.
nuance: Hegemony suggests influence that others come to accept as normal, while dominance is the broader, plainer word for any control.
prompt: For ten years, a single style of music has filled nearly every hour of radio airtime.
options: Pop ballads enjoyed a hegemony over the radio that left little airtime for any other style.
The hegemony of pop ballads meant that every genre on the radio got exactly equal airtime each day.
The trio's vocal hegemony was so sweet that their three voices blended into a single chord.
Her hegemony over the radio was limited to choosing the station in her own car.
reasons: One style crowding out all rivals across the airwaves is exactly this kind of sway.
Equal shares for all genres describes balance, the reverse of one style ruling.
This confuses the word with harmony; blended voices have nothing to do with dominance.
The word means sway over many others, not one person turning her own dial.

practice.prompt: In one region, a single art academy shaped what painters were taught for a century.
options: The academy's hegemony was so complete that young painters copied its rules without question.
Because the academy held hegemony, each painter chose freely among many styles that were all equally respected.
The gardener planted a hegemony of boxwood shrubs around the edge of the studio.
A shy student gained hegemony over the whole class simply by borrowing one brush.
reasons: Influence so widely accepted that nobody challenges it is the heart of the word.
Free choice among equal styles shows no single school leading the others.
This mistakes the word for hedge; it names a kind of dominance, not a row of plants.
Borrowing a single brush gives no one lasting leadership over a group.
